title: Leader-Based Replication
summary:
In leader-based (single-leader, primary-backup) replication **one replica, the leader, accepts all writes**; the others, the followers, copy its **replication log** and apply it in the same order. Because exactly one node decides the order of writes, replicas cannot disagree about write order, and there are no write-write conflicts to resolve between replicas.

Think of one editor with several proofreaders who only get copies: the editor's version is the truth, and copies lag by however long delivery takes.

What you get and what you pay:

- **Reads scale** by adding followers; **writes do not**. Every write still goes through the one leader (to scale writes, [shard](#/sd/f/sharding) as well).
- **Followers can be stale**, depending on sync or async replication.
- **Losing the leader** needs a [failover](#/sd/f/leader-based-failover), which risks lost writes and two leaders at once.

Common log formats: statement-based (breaks on `NOW()` or `RAND()`), physical WAL shipping (exact but version-coupled), and logical row-based (portable, the usual choice).

Adding a follower never pauses the leader: take a consistent snapshot tagged with its log position, copy it, then replay everything after that position.

The four sub-topics are the [write path](#/sd/f/leader-based-write-path), [read path](#/sd/f/leader-based-read-path), [consistency](#/sd/f/leader-based-consistency) and [failover](#/sd/f/leader-based-failover). Compare with [multi-leader](#/sd/f/multi-leader-replication) and [leaderless](#/sd/f/leaderless-replication).

drills.q: A primary database is at 95% CPU from write load (reads are only 5% of traffic). The team adds three followers. What is the expected effect?
options: Almost none: all writes still go through the one leader, so write capacity is unchanged
CPU on the leader halves because writes are split among replicas
Writes are now safe from conflicts
drills.explain: Followers copy the leader's work; they do not share it. They absorb reads. To scale writes you must shard the data or change the write path.

drills.q: A leader can commit at most 2,000 writes/s. The workload is 4% writes and 96% reads, and the followers can absorb all the reads. What is the maximum total request rate the system can sustain?
drills.explain: Writes are the bottleneck: total x 0.04 <= 2,000, so total <= 50,000 requests/s (of which 48,000 are reads on followers). Adding followers does not raise this ceiling.

drills.q: Order the steps of adding a new follower to a running leader without downtime.
items: Take a consistent snapshot of the leader and record its log position
Copy the snapshot to the new follower
The follower connects to the leader and requests all changes after the recorded position
The follower applies the backlog until it has caught up
The follower starts serving reads and following the live log
drills.explain: The log position is what makes the snapshot usable: without it you cannot tell which writes happened after the snapshot and would miss or double-apply changes.

drills.q: A leader ships statements (not row changes) to its followers. A write is `UPDATE jobs SET started_at = NOW() WHERE id = 5`. What can go wrong?
options: Each follower evaluates NOW() at its own time, so the replicas end up with different values
The statement is rejected by followers
drills.explain: Non-deterministic functions make statement-based replication diverge. Row-based (logical) logging ships the resulting values, so every replica stores the same data.

drills.q: Why does a single leader remove write-write conflicts between replicas, and what does that cost you?
drills.answer: All writes pass through one node, which assigns one total order that every follower replays, so replicas never see competing orders. The cost is that write throughput is bounded by one node and that losing it requires a failover.
